title: The Breton stripe (marinière)
body: A regulation of 27 March 1858 made the blue-and-white striped marinière part of the French Navy seamen's uniform, specifying 21 white stripes, each twice as wide as the navy stripes. It is called a Breton shirt because many French Navy sailors came from Brittany. During the First World War, Coco Chanel took inspiration from the local sailors' uniforms on seaside holidays, and the stripe moved from uniform to everyday fashion.

title: Paisley: the boteh motif
body: Paisley is built on the boteh (or buta), a teardrop-shaped motif with a curved upper end, of Iranian/Persian origin. It became popular in the West in the 18th and 19th centuries through imported Kashmir shawls from India, and was then copied locally. The English name comes from the town of Paisley in the west of Scotland, a textile centre where the designs were reproduced on Jacquard looms.

title: The kimono and its square sleeve
body: The kimono is a wrapped-front garment with square sleeves and a rectangular body, worn left side over right. It has a set method of construction and is usually cut from a long, narrow bolt of cloth called a tanmono. Before the Edo period (1603–1868), garments resembling the modern kimono, with narrow sleeve openings and hanging sleeves, were called kosode.

title: The aloha shirt
body: Sources trace the aloha shirt to Honolulu in the 1920s or early 1930s, when the store Musa-Shiya the Shirtmaker made shirts from colourful Japanese prints. Ellery Chun of King-Smith Clothiers in Waikiki is also credited, possibly as the first to sell them ready-to-wear off the shelf. The term "aloha shirt" first appeared in print in a Musa-Shiya advertisement in The Honolulu Advertiser on 28 June 1935. From 1962 the Hawaiian Fashion Guild promoted aloha shirts as workwear, the root of "Aloha Friday".

title: Tartan and the Dress Act
body: Tartan is cloth woven with crossing horizontal and vertical bands in several colours, forming a repeating pattern called a sett. It became a symbol of Scottish identity. After the Jacobite rising of 1745, the Dress Act 1746 banned Highland dress as part of the effort to weaken the clans. The ban was repealed in 1782, largely through the efforts of the Highland Society of London.

title: Ikat: patterned before weaving
body: Ikat, from a word meaning "to bind" in Malayo-Polynesian languages, is a Southeast Asian technique where the pattern is dyed into the yarns before the cloth is woven. Yarns are bound tightly in the desired pattern so the dye cannot reach the wrapped parts. In warp or weft ikat only one set of yarns is dyed; in double ikat both are. Similar but unrelated techniques developed independently in India, Central Asia and Japan.

title: Houndstooth check
body: Houndstooth is a two-tone pattern of solid light and dark checks alternating with diagonally striped checks. The contemporary check may have originated in woven wool tweed from the Scottish Lowlands, and is now woven in many fabrics besides wool.

title: The Peter Pan collar
body: A Peter Pan collar is flat, with rounded corners. It is named after the collar of Maude Adams's costume in her 1905 role as Peter Pan, designed by John White Alexander and his wife with Adams for the New York production of Peter and Wendy, although similar collars were worn before then.

title: Cotton: care and sewing notes
body: Cotton is a natural plant fibre that presses crisply and takes dye well. Untreated cotton can shrink on the first hot wash, so wash and dry a garment or patch fabric the way you will care for it before you cut. Use a universal machine needle and all-purpose thread; press seams with steam as you go.

title: Denim: care and sewing notes
body: Denim is a sturdy twill-weave cotton, usually with an indigo-dyed warp and a white weft, which is why it fades and shows wear on edges and seams. Wash it inside out in cold water to slow fading. Sew with a denim (jeans) needle and heavier topstitching thread, and go slowly over thick flat-felled seams.

title: Wool: care and mending notes
body: Wool is warm, springy and naturally resists creasing, but heat, agitation and soap together make it felt and shrink. Hand-wash cool, roll in a towel to remove water and dry flat. Moth holes and thin elbows are easy to darn with matching wool yarn.

title: Knits and jersey: sewing notes
body: Knit fabrics such as jersey stretch because they are made of interlocking loops, so they do not fray but can run or ripple when sewn. Use a ballpoint or stretch needle and a narrow zigzag or stretch stitch so seams can stretch with the fabric. Raw edges of jersey can be left unhemmed: they curl slightly instead of unravelling.

title: Polyester and blends: care notes
body: Polyester is a synthetic fibre that holds its shape, dries quickly and resists wrinkles, but melts under a hot iron. Press on a low setting with a pressing cloth. Synthetic fabrics shed microfibres when washed, so wash full loads at low temperature and less often.

title: Sashiko-mended denim jacket
body: Reinforce worn elbows, cuffs and pocket corners with a patch and rows of visible running stitch, so the repair becomes the detail.
tools: scrap of sturdy cotton or denim|sashiko or embroidery thread|long needle|pins|fabric chalk
steps: Find the worn areas and cut a patch 3 cm larger than each on every side|Pin the patch behind the worn area, inside the garment|Chalk parallel lines 6–8 mm apart across the patch|Sew along each line with an even running stitch, through both layers|Knot the thread ends on the inside and press lightly
result: The same denim jacket, whole and unchanged in shape, with square patches visible at the elbows, cuffs and pocket corners, each covered in neat parallel rows of white running stitch.

title: Cropped denim jacket
body: Shorten a long or boxy denim jacket to a cropped length by reattaching the waistband higher up.
tools: seam ripper|fabric chalk|scissors|sewing machine with denim needle|iron
steps: Try the jacket on and chalk the new length|Unpick the waistband from the body, keeping it whole|Cut the body to the chalk line plus 1.5 cm seam allowance|Shorten the front placket ends to match|Pin the waistband back on, sew it, and topstitch along the original stitch line|Press the seam toward the waistband
result: The same denim jacket shortened so the hem and waistband sit at the natural waist; collar, sleeves, pockets and buttons unchanged.

title: Denim jacket to vest
body: Remove the sleeves to turn a jacket into a layering vest, finishing the armholes with bias binding.
tools: seam ripper|scissors|bias binding|pins|sewing machine with denim needle|iron
steps: Unpick each sleeve at the armhole seam rather than cutting|Trim the armhole edge smooth, removing any thick seam allowance|Pin bias binding around each armhole, right sides together|Sew the binding, fold it to the inside and press|Topstitch the binding down from the outside
result: The same denim jacket as a sleeveless vest: no sleeves, both armholes finished with a narrow binding; collar, pockets and buttons unchanged.

title: Patchwork back panel on a denim jacket
body: Cover a stained or faded back panel with a patchwork of saved fabric scraps.
tools: fabric scraps|paper for a template|scissors|pins|sewing machine|iron
steps: Trace the jacket's back panel onto paper to make a template|Piece fabric scraps into a rectangle bigger than the template|Cut the patchwork to the template plus 1 cm on every side|Press the edges under by 1 cm|Pin it over the back panel and edge-stitch around it
result: The same denim jacket seen from the back, with the large back panel covered by a rectangle of pieced fabric scraps edge-stitched in place; everything else unchanged.

title: No-sew knotted shirt hem
body: Shorten and shape an oversized button shirt with a knot, without cutting or sewing.
steps: Button the shirt from the second button down|Undo the lowest two buttons|Lift the two front hem corners and tie them in a firm knot at your waist|Tuck the knot ends under and adjust the drape
result: The same button-up shirt, buttoned from the second button down, with the two front hem corners tied in a knot at the waist so the hem curves up at the front.

title: Band-collar shirt
body: Remove the collar leaf and keep the stand for a clean band (grandad) collar.
steps: Unpick the collar leaf from the top of the collar stand|Trim away the leaf, keeping the stand intact|Fold the stand's raw top edges inward by 1 cm and press|Pin the edges together|Edge-stitch along the top of the stand to close it
result: The same button-up shirt with the folded collar removed, leaving only a short upright band collar; everything else unchanged.

title: Cropped boxy shirt
body: Cut a long shirt to a boxy cropped length and finish with a narrow double hem.
steps: Try the shirt on and chalk the new hem|Lay it flat, buttoned, and cut 2 cm below the chalk line|Fold the raw edge under 1 cm, then 1 cm again, and press|Topstitch the hem close to the inner fold|Check the front edges line up when buttoned
result: The same button-up shirt cut to a short, boxy length ending above the waist, with a straight narrow hem; collar, sleeves and buttons unchanged.

title: Long sleeves to rolled short sleeves
body: Turn a long-sleeved shirt into a short-sleeved one with a stitched turn-up cuff.
steps: Chalk the finished length on each sleeve, then add 8 cm|Cut both sleeves at that line|Fold the raw edge up 1 cm and press|Fold up 3.5 cm twice to form the cuff and press|Tack the cuff at the underarm seam and the outer fold with a few hand stitches
result: The same button-up shirt with short sleeves ending above the elbow, each finished with a neat turned-up cuff; everything else unchanged.

title: No-sew T-shirt tote
body: Turn a T-shirt into a washable shopping tote with knotted fringe at the bottom.
steps: Lay the T-shirt flat and cut off both sleeves just inside the seams|Cut a scoop around the neckline to make the bag opening|Turn it inside out and cut 8 cm strips up from the hem, through both layers|Tie each front strip to the strip behind it with a double knot|Turn it right side out
result: Not a garment any more: a flat, open-top shopping bag made from the T-shirt body. The sleeves are cut away and the neckline scooped so the shoulders form two strap handles; the bottom edge is closed by a row of knotted fringe ties. The front of the shirt, with any print, is the front of the bag.

title: Cropped raw-hem T-shirt
body: Crop a T-shirt to a boxy length. Jersey does not fray, so the edge can stay raw.
steps: Try the T-shirt on and chalk the new length|Lay it flat and cut straight across through both layers|Gently stretch the cut edge so it rolls neatly|Wash once to set the rolled edge
result: The same T-shirt cut straight across to a short, boxy length ending above the waist, with a raw, slightly rolled edge; neckline and sleeves unchanged.

title: T-shirt to tank top
body: Cut off the sleeves and lower the armholes to make a relaxed tank.
tools: fabric chalk|scissors|sewing machine with ballpoint needle|iron
steps: Chalk a new armhole curve 4–5 cm inside and below the sleeve seam|Cut along the chalk line on both sides|Fold the armhole edge under 1 cm and pin|Sew with a narrow zigzag so the edge can stretch|Press lightly on a cool setting
result: The same T-shirt as a sleeveless tank top: sleeves removed and armholes cut deeper and curved, edges neatly turned; neckline, body and print unchanged.

title: Appliqué patch over a stain or faded graphic
body: Cover a mark or a cracked print with an appliqué cut from another worn-out garment.
tools: fusible web|fabric scraps|scissors|iron|sewing machine with ballpoint needle
steps: Iron fusible web onto the back of the patch fabric|Draw and cut out your shape|Peel off the backing and press the shape over the mark|Zigzag around the edge to secure it|Press again from the inside
result: The same T-shirt with one cut-fabric shape stitched flat onto the front, covering a small worn or stained area; shape and the rest of the shirt unchanged.

title: Visible darning on a sweater
body: Repair holes and thin elbows with a woven darn in a contrasting colour.
tools: darning mushroom or a smooth jar|wool yarn|blunt darning needle
steps: Stretch the hole gently over the darning mushroom|Sew vertical lines of yarn across the hole, anchoring 1 cm into solid knitting on each side|Weave horizontal lines over and under the vertical ones|Push each row snug against the last with the needle|Weave the yarn ends into the back of the knitting
result: The same sweater, whole and unchanged in shape, with small woven darned patches in a contrasting yarn at the elbows or over small holes.

title: Sweater to cardigan
body: Cut a pullover open down the front and finish it with a button band.
tools: sewing machine|fabric chalk|ruler|sharp scissors|grosgrain ribbon|buttons|needle and thread
steps: Fold the sweater in half and chalk the exact centre front|Sew two lines of short straight stitches 5 mm each side of the chalk line, twice, to lock the stitches|Cut between the stitched lines|Pin grosgrain ribbon along each cut edge on the inside and sew it down|Sew buttonholes on one side and buttons on the other
result: The same sweater opened down the centre front into a cardigan, with a ribbon-faced button band and a row of buttons; collar, sleeves and knit unchanged.

title: Cropped sweater
body: Shorten a long sweater and refinish the hem with the original ribbing.
steps: Cut off the ribbed hem band in one piece, just above the rib|Chalk the new length on the body and stitch a line of small zigzag 1 cm below it|Cut along the line beneath the zigzag|Pin the rib band back on, right sides together, stretching evenly|Sew with a narrow zigzag
result: The same sweater shortened to end above the waist, finished with its original ribbed hem band; neckline and sleeves unchanged.

title: Felted wool sweater bag
body: Shrink a 100% wool sweater on purpose so it felts, then cut it into a sturdy bag that will not unravel.
steps: Check the label is 100% wool; superwash or blends will not felt|Wash it hot with a little soap and tumble dry|Cut the body into a rectangle and the sleeves into two straps|Sew the bottom edge closed|Sew a strap inside each side of the opening
result: Not a garment any more: a small rectangular bag in dense, slightly fuzzy felted knit, with two strap handles made from the sleeves.

title: Trousers to cuffed shorts
body: Cut trousers or jeans to shorts with a stitched turn-up cuff.
steps: Try them on and chalk the finished length, then add 6 cm|Lay them flat and cut both legs straight across|Fold each leg up 3 cm twice and press|Tack each cuff at the side seams with a few hand stitches
result: The same trousers cut to shorts ending at mid-thigh, each leg finished with a neat double turned-up cuff; waistband and pockets unchanged.

title: Inside knee patch for jeans
body: Repair a knee hole from the inside so the frayed edge stays visible but strong.
steps: Cut a patch 4 cm larger than the hole on every side|Turn the leg inside out and pin the patch over the hole|Turn it back and sew rows of running stitch through both layers across the hole|Knot the thread ends inside
result: The same jeans, unchanged in shape, with a frayed knee opening backed from inside by a patch held with visible rows of running stitch.

title: Taper wide trouser legs
body: Slim the legs from the knee down by taking in the inseam.
steps: Turn the trousers inside out and try them on|Pin along the inseam from knee to hem to the fit you want|Chalk a smooth line from the knee down to the hem|Sew along the line and try them on again|Trim the excess to 1.5 cm, finish the edge with zigzag and press
result: The same trousers with the legs narrowed from the knee down to a slim tapered ankle; waistband, pockets and fabric unchanged.

title: Jeans to skirt
body: Unpick the inner leg seams and fill the gaps with a panel cut from the legs.
tools: seam ripper|scissors|pins|sewing machine with denim needle|iron
steps: Unpick both inseams and the crotch seam up to the fly|Cut the legs off at the length you want plus 3 cm|Lay the front flat, overlap the crotch so it lies straight, and pin|Cut a triangle from the leftover legs to fill the gap underneath and pin it in|Topstitch along the overlaps|Repeat on the back, then hem
result: Not trousers any more: a straight skirt made from the jeans, with the legs opened along the inner seams and triangular panels of the same denim filling the front and back; waistband and pockets unchanged.
